newsitem.title: USA: Secret Nazi gold for coal deal revealed. [CORRECTED 23:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Secret Nazi gold for coal deal revealed. [CORRECTED 23:25 GMT]

text.p: Portugal acquired looted Nazi gold worth about $1 billion at today's prices during the Second World War and tried to use it to buy coal from Poland in the brutal winter of 1946, according to previously confidential U.S. documents released on Tuesday.

The attempt to use the looted gold to buy Polish coal spurred a furious protest by the United States, Britain and France, which were trying to return it to its rightful owners including the treasuries of countries conquered by the Nazis.

The United States believed Lisbon held important amounts of gold from the Dutch and Belgian treasuries and one postwar State Department document complained that Portugal felt under no "obligation to return any German gold."

Another document, a Dec. 6, 1946 memorandum from the U.S. State Department, said the Portuguese admitted to receiving gold either directly from Germany or through Swiss middlemen acting as major launderers of Nazi assets during the war.

The World Jewish Congress, which has been searching the U.S. National Archives to trace Nazi assets, said it had reasons to believe the secret Polish coal deal was completed despite the Allied protests. The documents did not state how much the coal deal was worth.

A WJC spokesman said the group believed a significant commision was paid to a Swiss firm, which served as a middleman in the deal. The documents name the Nehaeba Coporation of Zurich as being prepared to buy the gold from Portugal so that Poland could be paid in Swiss francs.

The newly released documents also detail the movement of looted gold from the German Reichsbank through the Swiss National Bank to Portugal. By today's standards about $1 billion worth of gold went to Portugal, according to a WJC analysis of the documents.

A confidential State Department document on German gold movements said Germany started the war with estimated gold reserves of $100 million by 1940s prices and ended up looting $648 million from occupied countries. It said the Germans took $223 million from Belgium, $168 million from Holland and $64 million (Corrects from $464 million) from Italy, among other countries.

The discovery of the Portugal-Poland deal came two weeks after U.S. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato revealed another secret deal in which Switzerland agreed to turn over heirless assets of Holocaust victims to Poland as part of a plan to compensate Swiss citizens with claims against Poland.
